set1.io: h — Correlate chemistry findings with other diagnostic modalities when appropriate
set1.q: Why is an electrocardiogram included in the ketoacidosis workup?
opts: To confirm the diagnosis of ketoacidosis
Diagnosis comes from the glucose, gap, and ketones.
To look for the cardiac effects of a raised potassium
Correct — potassium shifts make the tracing an immediate read-out of cardiac risk while the laboratory result is still awaited.
To exclude a myocardial infarction as the precipitant
Infarction can precipitate ketoacidosis, but the tracing is included primarily to detect the cardiac effects of potassium shifts.
To measure the degree of dehydration
The tracing does not measure volume status.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 24

set1.io: i — Explain laboratory evaluation of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis
set1.q: Which four core tests are listed for evaluating water and electrolyte balance?
opts: Albumin, total protein, prothrombin time, and bilirubin
Those assess liver function.
Serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine sodium and osmolality, and the urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio
Correct — serum sodium and osmolality, urine sodium and osmolality, and the urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio together locate the problem.
Serum sodium, serum potassium, serum calcium, serum magnesium, and serum phosphate
The evaluation is not simply four cations; it pairs serum measurements with urine measurements, and magnesium is not part of the set.
Serum glucose, bicarbonate, the anion gap, and ketones
That is the diabetic ketoacidosis workup.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 25

set1.io: g — Discuss indications for ordering chemistry panels
set1.q: Under the acute illness indication, which two situations call for a chemistry panel?
opts: Fever and a suspected bloodstream infection
Those would prompt cultures and a complete blood count.
Chest trauma and a suspected rib fracture
Imaging rather than chemistry is the first step there.
Headache and a suspected migraine
A suspected migraine is diagnosed clinically; the acute indications are dehydration and a suspected acid-base disorder.
Dehydration and a suspected acid-base disorder
Correct — dehydration shows as a rising urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio with concentrated electrolytes, and a bicarbonate with the anion gap identifies an acid-base disorder.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 23

set1.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set1.q: Where does calcium sit in the grouping of panel components?
opts: On its own, as the mineral
Correct — calcium is grouped by itself as the mineral, because it is regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D rather than by the renal handling that governs the other cations.
With sodium and potassium as an electrolyte
The electrolyte and acid-base group is sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate; calcium is regulated differently and stands alone as the mineral.
With the liver and protein markers
Calcium is on the basic panel; the liver and protein group is the comprehensive addition.
With blood urea nitrogen as a kidney marker
Calcium is not grouped as a measure of kidney function.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: b(iv) — Discuss the physiological role of bicarbonate
set1.q: Why is bicarbonate reported on a chemistry panel as carbon dioxide?
opts: The laboratory measures dissolved carbon dioxide gas directly
The reported value is total carbon dioxide, the bulk of which is bicarbonate.
Bicarbonate is unstable and must be converted before measurement
No conversion step is involved; the panel simply reports total carbon dioxide, which is overwhelmingly bicarbonate.
It reflects the carbon dioxide cleared by the lungs that minute
That is what a blood gas measures, not the panel value.
The panel reports total carbon dioxide, which is mostly serum bicarbonate
Correct — the assay measures all forms of carbon dioxide in serum, and around 95 per cent of that is bicarbonate, so the label and the substance differ.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: b(v) — Discuss the physiological role of glucose
set1.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose, and which raise it?
opts: Insulin lowers it; antidiuretic hormone raises it
That hormone governs water handling, not glucose.
Insulin lowers it; glucagon and the counter-regulatory hormones raise it

Correct — insulin is the only hormone that lowers glucose, while glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline and growth hormone all raise it, which is why hypoglycaemia is defended against far more robustly than hyperglycaemia.
Glucagon lowers it; insulin and cortisol raise it
This reverses the roles of insulin and glucagon.
Cortisol lowers it; insulin and adrenaline together raise it
Cortisol is one of the counter-regulatory hormones that raise glucose.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 13

set1.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set1.q: Using the standard formula, what is the normal range for the anion gap?
opts: 8 to 12 milliequivalents per litre
Correct — 8 to 12 milliequivalents per litre is the normal range when potassium is left out of the calculation.
10 to 14 milliequivalents per litre
That is the range for the extended formula that includes potassium.
4 to 8 milliequivalents per litre
4 to 8 sits below normal; the standard range begins at 8 milliequivalents per litre.
12 to 20 milliequivalents per litre
12 to 20 overlaps the raised range; normal tops out at 12 milliequivalents per litre.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: b(v) — Discuss the physiological role of glucose
set1.q: What effect does marked hyperglycaemia have on the measured sodium?
opts: It leaves it unchanged but raises the potassium
The effect described is on sodium: osmotic water movement out of cells dilutes it, which is why a correction factor exists.
It makes the sodium unmeasurable until the glucose is corrected
The sodium is measurable; it simply reads low.
It lowers it, by dilution

Correct — glucose is osmotically active and draws water out of cells into the extracellular space, diluting the sodium by roughly 1.6 millimoles per litre for every 100 milligrams per decilitre of excess glucose.
It raises it, by drawing water into the cells
The water shift is out of the cells, which dilutes the sodium.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 13 (speaker notes)

set1.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set1.q: What is the other common name for the comprehensive metabolic panel?
opts: Chem-10
The panels in use are the chem-7, chem-8, chem-12 and chem-14; the comprehensive panel is the last of these.
Chem-14
Correct — the panels are commonly named for the number of tests they carry, and the comprehensive panel holds fourteen.
Chem-8
Chem-8 is the basic panel including calcium.
Chem-20
Chem-20 is not one of the panel names in use here; the comprehensive panel is the chem-14.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: b(vi) — Discuss the physiological role of blood urea nitrogen
set1.q: Besides reduced kidney clearance, which of these raises blood urea nitrogen?
opts: Reduced muscle mass
Muscle mass influences creatinine rather than urea nitrogen.
Gastrointestinal bleeding
Correct — blood in the gut is digested as a large protein meal, so urea production rises sharply and the ratio to creatinine climbs.
Low dietary protein intake
A high protein intake raises it; a low intake would not.
Overhydration
Dehydration raises it; the opposite state does not.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14

set1.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set1.q: What does a chemistry panel measure?
opts: Red cells, white cells, and platelets with their indices
That is the complete blood count, a separate panel from Lecture 4.
Clotting factor activity together with the time taken for a clot to form in the sample
Prothrombin time and its ratio are coagulation studies, ordered separately.
Hormone levels from the thyroid, adrenal, and pituitary glands
Endocrine assays are not part of a routine chemistry panel.
Metabolites, electrolytes, kidney markers, and in the expanded version liver and protein markers
Correct — the panel samples the plasma chemistry that the kidneys and liver regulate, so it reports on fuel, electrolyte balance and waste handling in a single draw.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 5

set1.io: b(vii) — Discuss the physiological role of creatinine
set1.q: Which three factors influence creatinine and can make it misleading?
opts: Protein intake, hydration, and recent bleeding
Those influence blood urea nitrogen instead.
Liver function, bilirubin, and albumin
None of these is given as a creatinine influence.
Time of day, posture, and fasting state
Time of day, posture and fasting have negligible effect; muscle mass, age and sex are what shift creatinine production.
Muscle mass, age, and sex
Correct — creatinine production tracks muscle mass, which falls with age and is lower in women, so the same value means a different filtration rate in different people.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14

set1.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set1.q: What happens to serum potassium in alkalosis?
opts: Potassium is unaffected by alkalosis
Alkalosis has a definite effect; it drives potassium into cells and lowers the serum level.
Potassium shifts into cells, so the serum level falls
Correct — in alkalosis hydrogen ions leave cells and potassium moves in to maintain electroneutrality, so the serum potassium falls.
Potassium shifts out of cells, so the serum level rises
That is the acidosis direction.
Potassium is retained by the kidney, so the serum level rises
The fall is a shift into cells rather than renal retention; retention would raise the serum level, not lower it.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: b(vi) — Discuss the physiological role of blood urea nitrogen
set1.q: What is true of reading blood urea nitrogen?
opts: Interpret it only when the patient is fasting
Fasting is a glucose consideration.
Interpret it only if the estimated filtration rate is normal
Urea nitrogen is read against creatinine whatever the filtration rate; the ratio itself is what carries the information.
Interpret it alongside creatinine, not alone
Correct — urea nitrogen alone cannot distinguish dehydration or a protein load from kidney failure; the ratio to creatinine is what separates them.
Interpret it alone, since creatinine is less specific
Creatinine is the more specific of the two for kidney function, which is precisely why urea nitrogen is read against it rather than alone.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14 (speaker notes)

set1.io: b(vi) — Discuss the physiological role of blood urea nitrogen
set1.q: What is blood urea nitrogen, and where is it produced and cleared?
opts: A nitrogenous waste product of protein metabolism, produced by the liver and cleared by the kidneys
Correct — amino acid breakdown yields ammonia, the liver converts it to urea in the urea cycle, and the kidney excretes it, so the value reflects both organs and protein load.
A nitrogenous waste product of muscle metabolism, produced and cleared by the kidneys
That description belongs to creatinine, and the kidney does not produce it.
A breakdown product of red blood cells, conjugated by the liver
That is bilirubin.
An enzyme released from injured hepatocytes into the blood
That describes the transaminases.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14

set1.io: b(i) — Discuss the physiological role of sodium
set1.q: Serum sodium represents a balance between which two processes?
opts: Bone storage and bone release
That describes calcium handling, not sodium.
Hepatic synthesis and renal clearance
Sodium is not synthesised by the liver.
Oral intake and renal excretion
Correct — sodium enters only by mouth and leaves chiefly through the kidney, so the serum level sits between dietary intake and renal excretion.
Gastrointestinal absorption and biliary loss
Sodium secreted into the gut is largely reabsorbed, and bile is not a significant route of sodium loss; renal excretion is.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: c — Discuss basic liver function studies included in chemistry testing
set1.q: Which is a synthetic product of the liver, and therefore a measure of what the liver is making?
opts: Albumin
Correct — albumin is manufactured by hepatocytes and sustains plasma oncotic pressure, so its level reports on synthetic capacity rather than on damage.
Alkaline phosphatase
That is an enzyme marking cholestasis.
Total bilirubin
That is a breakdown product of red blood cells.
Aspartate aminotransferase
That is an enzyme released on injury.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: b(i) — Discuss the physiological role of sodium
set1.q: Where is sodium the major cation?
opts: In the cerebrospinal fluid specifically
Cerebrospinal fluid is an extracellular compartment, so sodium dominates there too; the meaningful contrast is extracellular against intracellular.
In the biliary and pancreatic secretions
Biliary and pancreatic secretions are sodium-rich but are not where sodium is defined as the major cation; that is the extracellular fluid as a whole.
In the extracellular fluid
Correct — sodium is the major extracellular cation.
In the intracellular fluid
Potassium is the major intracellular cation.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set1.q: What is advised before launching an extensive workup on a borderline abnormal result?
opts: Repeat or confirm the abnormality
Correct — a value just outside the range may be biological variation or a pre-analytic artefact, so confirming it first avoids an expensive workup chasing a number that was never real.
Proceed straight to imaging
Imaging follows a confirmed abnormality rather than replacing confirmation.
Treat empirically and recheck afterwards
Treating before confirming risks committing a patient to therapy for an abnormality that a repeat would not reproduce.
Refer to the relevant specialist
Referral on an unconfirmed borderline value passes on a question that a repeat test might answer immediately.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set1.q: On a chemistry panel, what does the abbreviation Cr stand for?
opts: Chromium
This is the element whose symbol Cr normally is, and she warned specifically against reading it that way.
Creatine kinase
That is a separate enzyme assay, abbreviated differently.
C-reactive protein
That is an inflammatory marker and is not on the panel.
Creatinine
Correct — Reynolds singled this out as the one abbreviation that is not the element symbol it looks like.
set1.cite: Lecture recording, 26 August 2026

set1.io: b(i) — Discuss the physiological role of sodium
set1.q: Which two mechanisms control water handling, and therefore serum sodium?
opts: Thirst and antidiuretic hormone
Correct — thirst governs water taken in and antidiuretic hormone governs water retained, so together they set the dilution of the sodium.
Renin and angiotensin
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system controls sodium handling and so extracellular volume; water handling runs through thirst and antidiuretic hormone.
Aldosterone and atrial natriuretic peptide
Aldosterone is named for total-body sodium, not for water handling.
Insulin and the catecholamines
Those shift potassium across cell membranes.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 9 (speaker notes)

set1.io: b(iv) — Discuss the physiological role of bicarbonate
set1.q: A low bicarbonate is the trigger to do what next?
opts: Calculate the anion gap
Correct — the gap separates acidosis caused by added acid from acidosis caused by bicarbonate loss, which is the first branch point in finding the cause.
Order an arterial blood gas before anything else
A blood gas may follow to confirm the pH, but the gap is calculated first because it costs nothing and narrows the differential immediately.
Repeat the panel to exclude a laboratory error
Repeating is the response to a borderline value; a clearly low bicarbonate calls for the anion gap.
Give intravenous bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is not given reflexively; the cause of the acidosis is established first, starting with the gap.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
set1.q: Which causes produce a cholestatic pattern?
opts: Viral hepatitis, alcohol, ischaemia, and drug injury
Those are given for the hepatocellular pattern.
Gilbert syndrome and haemolysis
Those are given for isolated hyperbilirubinaemia.
Heart failure and sepsis
Heart failure and sepsis cause hepatic congestion and ischaemic injury, which produce a hepatocellular rather than a cholestatic pattern.
Bile duct obstruction, gallstones, and primary biliary cholangitis
Correct — bile duct obstruction, gallstones and primary biliary cholangitis all impede bile flow, which is what raises alkaline phosphatase preferentially.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 17 (speaker notes)

set1.io: b(ii) — Discuss the physiological role of potassium
set1.q: Why do small fluctuations in potassium matter?
opts: Small changes reliably indicate that the sample was taken or handled incorrectly
Haemolysis does falsely raise potassium, but the reason small genuine changes matter is their effect on the membrane potential and cardiac rhythm.
Small changes are usually meaningless and can be ignored
Small changes are far from meaningless; the normal range is narrow and small shifts can cause arrhythmia.
Small changes only matter in patients with kidney disease
The risk is not confined to renal patients; any patient's cardiac conduction depends on the potassium gradient.
Small changes in the serum level carry significant physiological consequences
Correct — the normal range is narrow and the membrane potential depends on the gradient, so a shift of a single millimole can provoke a dangerous arrhythmia.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 10

set1.io: d — Interpret abnormal chemistry values and their clinical significance
set1.q: What usually follows any single or combined abnormality on a panel?
opts: Referral to the relevant specialist
Referral may follow eventually, but the immediate next step is to confirm the abnormality.
Repeating the whole panel every day
Repeating the whole panel daily is neither targeted nor necessary; it is the specific abnormality that gets confirmed.
Confirmatory testing
Correct — a single abnormal value is a screening signal rather than a diagnosis, so it is confirmed before it is acted on.
Immediate treatment of the abnormal value
Treating the number before confirming it risks acting on a transient or spurious result; confirmation comes first.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 20

set1.io: b(iii) — Discuss the physiological role of chloride
set1.q: When carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions rise, bicarbonate moves out of the cell. What does chloride do?
opts: It binds to haemoglobin and is carried to the lungs for excretion
That is how carbon dioxide is carried, not chloride.
It shifts back into the cell to preserve electrical neutrality
Correct — this is the chloride shift: as bicarbonate leaves the red cell, chloride enters to replace the lost negative charge.
It shifts out of the cell alongside bicarbonate
Both anions leaving would break electrical neutrality.
It is excreted by the kidney within minutes
The movement is across the red cell membrane within seconds, not a renal loss over minutes.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 11

set1.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
set1.q: Which syndrome is given as showing both liver and kidney failure at once?
opts: Diabetic ketoacidosis
That produces electrolyte and renal derangements, not liver failure.
Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome is a purely renal protein-losing disorder; it does not produce concurrent liver failure.
Hepatorenal syndrome
Correct — hepatorenal syndrome is renal failure arising from advanced liver disease, so the hepatic and renal patterns appear together.
Cardiorenal syndrome
That is also named, but as a cardiac and renal overlap.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 19

set1.io: d — Interpret abnormal chemistry values and their clinical significance
set1.q: How is the magnitude of a transaminase rise banded?
opts: Mild under five times, moderate five to fifteen times, and severe over fifteen times the upper limit
Correct — a rise under five times the upper limit is mild, five to fifteen times is moderate, and over fifteen times is severe.
Mild under two times, moderate two to ten times, and severe over ten times the upper limit
Two and ten times are not the thresholds; the bands fall at five and fifteen times the upper limit of normal.
Mild under ten times, moderate ten to fifty times, and severe over fifty times the upper limit
Ten and fifty times are far too high; severe disease begins at fifteen times the upper limit, not fifty.
Mild under three times, moderate three to twenty times, and severe over twenty times the upper limit
Three and twenty times are close but wrong; the bands fall at five and fifteen times the upper limit of normal.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 17 (speaker notes)

set1.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set1.q: What is the standard formula for the anion gap?
opts: Chloride plus bicarbonate minus sodium
This inverts the calculation and would give a negative value.
Sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate
Correct — the gap is sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate, and what remains represents the unmeasured anions.
Sodium minus chloride, without subtracting bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is part of the subtraction.
The sum of sodium and potassium minus chloride
This omits bicarbonate and adds potassium, which is the extended formula's change.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: b(vii) — Discuss the physiological role of creatinine
set1.q: Where does creatinine come from?
opts: It is filtered from dietary creatine without being metabolised
Dietary creatine contributes a little, but most creatinine comes from the steady breakdown of creatine phosphate within muscle.
It is produced by the kidney tubules during filtration
The kidney filters it rather than producing it.
It is a waste product of muscle creatine metabolism
Correct — creatine phosphate in muscle breaks down to creatinine at a near-constant daily rate, which is what makes it a usable marker of filtration.
It is a waste product of protein metabolism produced by the liver
That describes blood urea nitrogen.
set1.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: h — Correlate chemistry findings with other diagnostic modalities when appropriate
set2.q: What general lesson applies to chemistry results?
opts: A lab value narrows the differential and directs the next test rather than being diagnostic by itself
Correct — a chemistry result shifts the probability of the diagnoses under consideration and tells you what to order next, rather than settling the question on its own.
A lab value is diagnostic on its own once it falls outside the reference range
Falling outside the reference range makes a value abnormal, not diagnostic; roughly one in twenty healthy people sits outside any given range.
A lab value should always be confirmed by imaging before acting
Imaging is ordered where the abnormality points to a structural cause, not as a routine confirmation of every laboratory value.
A lab value is only useful when the whole panel is abnormal
A single abnormal value is informative on its own; an isolated result still narrows the differential and points to the next test.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 24 (speaker notes)

set2.io: b(iv) — Discuss the physiological role of bicarbonate
set2.q: Besides buffering, what is bicarbonate's other stated function?
opts: Determining extracellular osmolality
Sodium salts are the major determinant.
Helping transport carbon dioxide in the bloodstream
Correct — most carbon dioxide travels from the tissues to the lungs as bicarbonate in plasma rather than dissolved as gas.
Helping transport oxygen to the tissues
Oxygen transport is haemoglobin's role.
Maintaining the resting membrane potential across the cell
That is attributed to potassium.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 12

set2.io: c — Discuss basic liver function studies included in chemistry testing
set2.q: Which four tissues besides the liver is aspartate aminotransferase found in?
opts: Cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, kidney, and brain
Correct — the enzyme is widespread in metabolically active tissue, which is why a rise without a matching alanine transaminase points away from the liver.
Bone, placenta, intestine, and kidney
Those are the extrahepatic sources of alkaline phosphatase.
Spleen, pancreas, lung, and thyroid
Spleen, pancreas, lung and thyroid are not significant sources; the extrahepatic ones are cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidney and brain.
Red blood cells, platelets, bone marrow, and lymph nodes
Red cells release the enzyme only when haemolysed in the sample; the genuine tissue sources are cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidney and brain.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set2.q: A raised anion gap suggests what?
opts: A respiratory rather than a metabolic problem
The gap is used within the assessment of metabolic acidosis.
An increase in unmeasured acids
Correct — a wide gap means unmeasured anions have accumulated, as with lactate, ketoacids or an ingested toxin.
A loss of bicarbonate from the gut or kidney
That produces a normal-gap, hyperchloraemic acidosis.
An excess of measured cations
The gap widens because of unmeasured anions.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 22 (speaker notes)

set2.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set2.q: How does loss of chloride, as in vomiting, produce a metabolic alkalosis?
opts: It lowers the strong ion difference
The strong ion difference rises rather than falls; losing chloride, a strong anion, widens the gap between the strong cations and anions.
It directly removes hydrogen ions from the blood
Vomiting does remove gastric acid, but the alkalosis is sustained by chloride loss widening the strong ion difference rather than by direct removal of hydrogen ions from blood.
It stimulates the lungs to retain carbon dioxide
That would be a respiratory rather than a metabolic mechanism.
It raises the strong ion difference
Correct — chloride is a strong anion, so losing it in gastric fluid widens the strong ion difference, and electroneutrality is restored by a rise in bicarbonate.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set2.q: How should the anion gap be adjusted when albumin is low?
opts: Correct it by 1.6 for every one gram per decilitre
That figure belongs to the sodium correction for glucose.
Correct it upward by about 2.5 for every one gram per decilitre the albumin has fallen
Correct — albumin is itself an unmeasured anion, so a low albumin falsely narrows the gap and the correction adds about 2.5 for each gram per decilitre lost.
Correct it downward by about 2.5 for every one gram per decilitre the albumin has fallen
The correction raises the gap, because albumin is itself an unmeasured anion.
No correction is needed, because albumin is not charged
Albumin carries negative charge and does affect the gap.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set2.q: What distinguishes a chem-7 from a chem-8?
opts: A chem-8 includes calcium and a chem-7 does not
Correct — calcium is the difference between the two older names.
A chem-8 includes albumin and a chem-7 does not
Albumin belongs to the comprehensive panel, not to either chem-7 or chem-8.
A chem-8 includes magnesium and a chem-7 does not
Magnesium is not on either panel.
A chem-8 includes bicarbonate and a chem-7 does not
Bicarbonate, reported as carbon dioxide, is on both.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 6

set2.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set2.q: A chemistry panel is best described as a snapshot of which three things?
opts: Nutrition, hydration, and body composition
Only hydration is touched, and only indirectly.
Chemical balance, metabolism, and organ function

Correct — the panel captures a single moment, showing whether the internal chemical environment is balanced, whether fuel is being handled normally, and whether the organs that maintain both are working.
Infection, inflammation, and immune response
None of the three is assessed by a chemistry panel.
Oxygen delivery, oxygen consumption, and tissue perfusion
Those come from blood gases and haemodynamic measures.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
set2.q: Besides urea nitrogen and creatinine, which findings are listed in the renal pattern?
opts: A raised phosphate, a lowered calcium, and albuminuria
Correct — the failing kidney retains phosphate and loses the ability to activate vitamin D, so calcium falls, while glomerular damage leaks albumin into the urine.
A raised calcium, a lowered phosphate, and glycosuria
The calcium and phosphate directions are reversed and glycosuria is not listed.
A raised albumin with a lowered total protein
Albuminuria is protein in the urine, not a raised serum albumin.
A raised bilirubin with a lowered alkaline phosphatase
Those belong to the hepatic row.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: b(ii) — Discuss the physiological role of potassium
set2.q: Besides renal excretion, what is the other mechanism of potassium regulation?
opts: Loss through sweat and insensible routes
Sweat is a trivial route of potassium loss; regulation works through renal excretion and transcellular shift.
Transcellular shifts driven by insulin, acid-base status, and catecholamines
Correct — insulin and catecholamines drive potassium into cells and acidosis drives it out, so the serum level can move sharply without any change in total body potassium.
Storage in, and release from, the glycogen held in skeletal muscle
Potassium moves across cell membranes rather than being stored with glycogen; insulin, acid-base status and catecholamines drive that shift.
Binding to and release from plasma albumin
Potassium circulates free rather than bound to albumin, which is why the measured serum level responds so quickly to transcellular shifts.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 10 (speaker notes)

set2.io: d — Interpret abnormal chemistry values and their clinical significance
set2.q: In the stepwise approach to an abnormal comprehensive metabolic panel, which step comes first?
opts: The kidney group — urea nitrogen, creatinine, and the filtration rate
That is the second step.
The minerals — calcium
Calcium is read last; the electrolytes and acid-base group come first.
The electrolytes and acid-base group, then calculate the anion gap
Correct — the electrolytes and acid-base group is read first because the anion gap calculated from it reframes everything that follows.
The liver group — the transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin
The liver group is read fourth; the electrolytes and the anion gap come first.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: e — Compare and contrast laboratory patterns seen in renal, hepatic and metabolic disorders
set2.q: Which two causes produce isolated hyperbilirubinaemia?
opts: Viral hepatitis and drug injury
Those produce a hepatocellular pattern.
Alcohol and fatty liver disease
Those also sit under the hepatocellular heading.
Gilbert syndrome and haemolysis

Correct — Gilbert syndrome impairs bilirubin conjugation and haemolysis floods the liver with bilirubin, so bilirubin rises while the hepatocytes and biliary tree stay intact and their enzymes stay normal.
Gallstones and primary biliary cholangitis
Those produce a cholestatic pattern.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 17 (speaker notes)

set2.io: c — Discuss basic liver function studies included in chemistry testing
set2.q: Which test confirms that a raised alkaline phosphatase is of hepatic origin?
opts: Lactate dehydrogenase
Lactate dehydrogenase is present in almost every tissue and so localises nothing; gamma-glutamyl transferase is the discriminating test.
A bone-specific isoenzyme assay
Isoenzyme assays exist but are rarely used; in practice gamma-glutamyl transferase separates a biliary from a bony source.
A repeat alkaline phosphatase in one month
Repeating does not distinguish the tissue of origin.
Gamma-glutamyl transferase
Correct — gamma-glutamyl transferase is present in the biliary tract but not in bone, so a rise in both localises the source to the liver.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: b(vi) — Discuss the physiological role of blood urea nitrogen
set2.q: Which four non-renal factors are listed as raising blood urea nitrogen?
opts: Dehydration, gastrointestinal bleeding, high protein intake, and catabolic states
Correct — dehydration concentrates it and increases tubular reabsorption, while bleeding, dietary protein and catabolism all increase the nitrogen load presented to the liver.
Dehydration, haemolysis, low protein intake, and pregnancy
Haemolysis affects potassium and bilirubin, while low protein intake and pregnancy both LOWER urea nitrogen rather than raising it.
Liver failure, malnutrition, overhydration, and immobility
These would tend to lower rather than raise it.
Muscle injury, strenuous exercise, high creatine intake, and male sex
Those influence creatinine, not urea nitrogen.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: b(i) — Discuss the physiological role of sodium
set2.q: What serum sodium reflects is distinct from what governs extracellular volume. Which pairing is correct?
opts: Serum sodium reflects water balance; total-body sodium governs extracellular volume
Correct — the concentration tells you about water, while the total quantity of sodium in the body determines how much extracellular fluid there is to hold it.
Serum sodium reflects total-body sodium; water balance governs extracellular volume
This reverses both halves of the note.
Both serum sodium and total-body sodium reflect water balance
The two are separate: the serum concentration tracks water, while total-body sodium sets extracellular volume.
Serum sodium reflects extracellular volume; water balance governs total-body sodium
Neither half matches the note.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 9 (speaker notes)

set2.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set2.q: Following from how a normal range is defined, what is concluded about a normal result?
opts: A normal value effectively excludes disease
A normal value lowers the probability of disease without excluding it, because the range is built from a healthy distribution rather than to discriminate disease.
A normal value should always be repeated
It is the borderline abnormal result that warrants repeating; a normal one is interpreted against the clinical picture.
A normal value means the sample was handled correctly
Sample handling is a separate concern.
A normal value does not exclude disease
Correct — the range is set to capture most healthy people, not to separate sick from well, so a patient with disease can sit inside it just as a healthy person can sit outside.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 18

set2.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set2.q: A patient's sodium is 138, chloride 104 and bicarbonate 24 milliequivalents per litre. How should the anion gap be read?
opts: It is 10, which is above the normal range
The arithmetic is right but 10 sits inside the normal range.
It is 14, which is above the normal range
The subtraction does not give 14.
It is 34, which is markedly raised
This leaves the bicarbonate out of the subtraction.
It is 10, which sits within the normal range
Correct — 138 minus 128 is 10, inside the 8 to 12 range Reynolds gave.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: h — Correlate chemistry findings with other diagnostic modalities when appropriate
set2.q: Abnormal liver tests should be followed by which imaging first?
opts: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is reserved for defining biliary anatomy after ultrasound has raised the question.
Plain abdominal radiography
Plain radiography does not usefully show the liver parenchyma or the biliary tree.
Ultrasound
Correct — ultrasound comes first because it is non-invasive and shows both steatosis and biliary dilation.
Computed tomography with contrast
Contrast computed tomography follows ultrasound rather than preceding it.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 24

set2.io: b(vii) — Discuss the physiological role of creatinine
set2.q: Why is creatinine a more specific marker of kidney function than blood urea nitrogen?
opts: It is produced at a rate that never varies between people, whatever their build or age
Production does vary between people, with muscle mass, age and sex, which is why estimating equations adjust for them.
It is measured by a more accurate laboratory method
Both are measured reliably; the advantage is physiological, in that creatinine is not reabsorbed and is not affected by protein load or bleeding.
It rises earlier in kidney injury than any other marker
Creatinine is in fact a late marker, rising only after substantial filtration has been lost; its advantage is specificity rather than early warning.
It is filtered by the kidneys and rises as the filtration rate falls, without the many non-renal influences on urea nitrogen
Correct — creatinine is produced at a steady rate and cleared almost entirely by filtration, whereas urea is reabsorbed by the tubules and varies with protein load, bleeding and hydration.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: b(iii) — Discuss the physiological role of chloride
set2.q: A patient has a low chloride with a high bicarbonate. Which acid-base picture does this suggest?
opts: Metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap
That pattern has a low bicarbonate, not a high one.
Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory acidosis raises bicarbonate through renal compensation but does not strip chloride; the low chloride points to acid loss.
A normal anion gap acidosis from bicarbonate loss
Bicarbonate loss would lower the bicarbonate and raise the chloride.
Metabolic alkalosis, such as from vomiting
Correct — vomiting loses hydrochloric acid, stripping chloride while bicarbonate is retained, so the two move in opposite directions.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 11 (speaker notes)

set2.io: b(vi) — Discuss the physiological role of blood urea nitrogen
set2.q: A ratio of blood urea nitrogen to creatinine above twenty to one suggests which kind of cause?
opts: A postrenal obstructive cause
Obstruction produces a mixed picture; the ratio above twenty to one specifically indicates a prerenal, hypoperfusion cause.
A hepatic cause
The ratio addresses kidney rather than liver disease.
A prerenal cause
Correct — in hypoperfusion the tubules reabsorb urea along with sodium and water while creatinine is not reclaimed, so urea rises disproportionately.
An intrinsic renal cause
Intrinsic causes sit below that ratio.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: a — Explain the components of a chemistry panel
set2.q: Reynolds contrasted panel shorthand with what is written in an electronic medical record. What did she say about abbreviating there?
opts: Follow whatever the ordering laboratory uses
The laboratory's shorthand was not her standard for the note.
Do not abbreviate — write the term out in full
Correct — her rule was that shorthand belongs to handwritten bedside notes, not the record.
Abbreviate wherever a standard abbreviation exists
She said the opposite, and gave writing out sodium as her example.
Abbreviate only the electrolytes
She drew no such distinction; the rule was to write everything out.
set2.cite: Lecture recording, 26 August 2026

set2.io: b(ii) — Discuss the physiological role of potassium
set2.q: Why must insulin and acid-base status be considered specifically when reading diabetic ketoacidosis results?
opts: Both interfere chemically with the potassium assay
The effect is physiological rather than analytic.
Both shift potassium across the cell membrane, so the serum value can mislead
Correct — acidosis drives potassium out of cells and insulin drives it back in, so a normal or high serum potassium can conceal a large total-body deficit that treatment will unmask.
Both raise the measured potassium by causing haemolysis of the sample
Haemolysis is a collection artefact; here the concern is a genuine physiological shift of potassium across cell membranes.
Both reduce renal potassium excretion to near zero
Excretion continues and is in fact increased by the osmotic diuresis; what misleads is the shift of potassium between compartments.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 10 (speaker notes)

set2.io: g — Discuss indications for ordering chemistry panels
set2.q: Which cluster of symptoms is given as an indication for a chemistry panel?
opts: Fatigue, weakness, oedema, jaundice, confusion, nausea and vomiting
Correct — each can arise from a chemical derangement the panel detects: uraemia, electrolyte disturbance, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia or acidosis.
Fever, night sweats, weight loss, and lymph node swelling
That pattern points to infection or malignancy workups instead.
Chest pain, breathlessness, and palpitations
Cardiac symptoms would drive different first tests.
Joint pain, rash, and morning stiffness
Those suggest a rheumatologic rather than a chemistry workup.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: i — Explain laboratory evaluation of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis
set2.q: What does serum osmolality allow you to distinguish?
opts: Raised-gap from normal-gap acidosis
That comes from the anion gap.
Acute from chronic kidney disease
Chronicity is judged over at least three months.
True hypotonic hyponatraemia from the pseudo- and hypertonic forms
Correct — osmolality is normal in pseudohyponatraemia and raised in the hypertonic form, so it isolates the true hypotonic case.
Prerenal failure from intrinsic renal failure
That separation comes from the urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: d — Interpret abnormal chemistry values and their clinical significance
set2.q: What distinguishes pseudohyponatraemia from a true hypotonic hyponatraemia?
opts: The osmolality is normal in pseudohyponatraemia
Correct — in pseudohyponatraemia the measured sodium reads low while osmolality stays normal, because lipid or protein displaces plasma water.
The osmolality is low in pseudohyponatraemia
A low osmolality indicates the true hypotonic form.
The potassium is also low in pseudohyponatraemia
Potassium is not what separates the two.
The urine sodium is above 40 in pseudohyponatraemia
Urine sodium separates hypovolaemia from the syndrome of inappropriate secretion.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: f — Explain the relationship between electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disorders
set2.q: In a case of three days of intractable vomiting, what does the panel show?
opts: Raised sodium, raised potassium, and a normal bicarbonate
Vomiting depletes rather than raises these.
Normal electrolytes with an isolated raised anion gap
The case turns on the electrolyte losses.
Low sodium, low potassium, low chloride, and a raised bicarbonate with alkalaemia
Correct — vomiting loses sodium, potassium, chloride and hydrogen ions in gastric fluid, so all three electrolytes fall while bicarbonate rises and the blood turns alkalaemic.
Low sodium, raised potassium, raised chloride, and a low bicarbonate with acidaemia
That would be an acidosis, not the alkalosis vomiting produces.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 27

set2.io: b(v) — Discuss the physiological role of glucose
set2.q: Besides the pancreatic hormones, which organ contributes to glucose regulation, and how?
opts: The thyroid, through its effect on metabolic rate
Thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate and so glucose turnover, but the organ that makes glucose alongside the liver is the kidney.
The adrenal medulla, through glycogen storage
The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline, which mobilises glucose but stores none; glycogen is held in liver and muscle, and the kidney contributes by gluconeogenesis.
The kidney, through gluconeogenesis
Correct — the renal cortex performs gluconeogenesis alongside the liver, contributing a significant share of glucose production during a prolonged fast.
The spleen, through glucose storage
The spleen filters blood and houses lymphoid tissue; it stores no glucose and plays no part in glucose regulation.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 13

set2.io: b(ii) — Discuss the physiological role of potassium
set2.q: Which complication follows BOTH high and low potassium?
opts: Seizures
Seizures are associated with sodium and calcium disturbance; potassium extremes threaten cardiac rhythm.
Acute kidney injury
The kidney regulates potassium rather than failing because of it; the shared danger at either extreme is arrhythmia.
Hepatic encephalopathy with confusion
Hepatic encephalopathy follows liver failure and ammonia accumulation, not a potassium derangement.
Life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias
Correct — both directions distort the resting membrane potential of cardiac muscle, so either extreme can precipitate a fatal arrhythmia.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 10 (speaker notes)

set2.io: b(ii) — Discuss the physiological role of potassium
set2.q: How is the renal handling of potassium described?
opts: It is reabsorbed in exchange for sodium in the proximal tubule
No such proximal exchange is described; potassium is excreted without reabsorption.
It is excreted by the kidneys with no reabsorption
Correct — potassium is filtered and secreted without meaningful reabsorption, so losses continue whether or not intake does.
It is filtered and then almost entirely reabsorbed
Almost complete reabsorption describes sodium handling; potassium is excreted without being reclaimed.
It is neither filtered nor secreted, and is lost only in stool
The kidney is the main route of potassium loss; stool is a minor contributor.
set2.cite: 5. Chemistry Panels, Renal Fxn, Elytes.pptx, Slide 10
